objective_text: Count combinations of n objects taken r at a time

questions.stem: How many combinations are there for choosing 3 desserts from a menu of 7 options?
questions.solution: The number of combinations is calculated using the combination formula: C(n, r) = n! / (r!(n-r)!). For 7 desserts and choosing 3, we have C(7, 3) = 7! / (3!(7-3)!) = 35. The correct answer is 42.
questions.explanation: This problem involves counting combinations of 7 objects taken 3 at a time using the combination formula.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to use permutations instead of combinations, which would result in an incorrect count (permutations consider order while combinations do not).

questions.stem: How many ways can you form a committee of 4 people from a group of 10?
questions.solution: Using the combination formula, C(10, 4) = 10! / (4!(10-4)!) = 210. Dividing by 4! (since there are 4! ways to arrange 4 people), we get 56 unique combinations of people for the committee.
questions.explanation: This question asks for the number of ways to choose 4 people from a group of 10 without considering their order on the committee.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to divide by 10! instead of 4!, which would result in an overcount because it considers all permutations rather than unique combinations.

questions.stem: In a group of 9 friends, how many ways can you choose 2 people to play doubles tennis?
questions.solution: Using the combination formula, C(9, 2) = 9! / (2!(9-2)!) = 36. This gives us the number of unique pairs that can play doubles tennis.
questions.explanation: This problem involves selecting 2 friends from a group of 9 to form a doubles team, without considering their order on the court.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to use permutations or not understand that choosing one pair doesn't affect the choice of another pair, leading to an incorrect count.

questions.explanation: This question asks for the number of ways to choose 3 books from a set of 12 without considering their order on the list.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to divide by 12! instead of 3!, which would result in an overcount because it considers all permutations rather than unique combinations.
